decisions.quote: Discussion Summary of Replication Attempt In the current study, we attempted to replicate the primary result of Study 5from Reynolds & Besner (2008), wherein there was no delay in responding when switching between stimulus categories while reading words and nonwords aloud. This effect was produced at two levels of analysis – participant-level, and stimulus item-level. In our replication with high power and a similar sample, we partially replicated the original results. We conducted both participant- level and item-level analyses and found that there was no significant evidence for a switch cost at the participant-level, but there was a switch cost when the data was analyzed at an item level. Lastly, there was an unexpected interaction between switch cost and stimulus type (i.e., word or nonword) when the data was analyzed at the participant level but not at the stimulus item level. Participants read words more slowly after a switch, but read nonwords at a similar speed regardless of whether there was a switch. In contrast to the reaction-time results, we fully replicated the error rate results from Study 5.

decisions.quote: Regarding the primary finding, we detected a statistically significant effect of nearness, F (1, 29) = 8.064, p = .008, partial η2 = .218, whereby words with many near neighbors were categorized more slowly than words with few near neighbors. We failed to detect a statistically significant effect for distant neighbors, F (1, 29) = 1.562, p = .221, partial η2 = .051. In addition, we failed to detect a statistically significant interaction effect, F (1, 29) = 3.192, p = .084, partial η2 = .099. Discussion Summary of Replication Attempt The present findings indicate a successful replication attempt in terms of statistical significance. Specifically, a statistically “significant” (i.e., p < .01) effect of nearness in the predicted direction was found in our replication study, replicating what was observed in the original study. However, the observed effect size in our replication (partial η2 = .22) was smaller than the effect size observed in the original study (partial η2 = .45).

decisions.quote: Discussion The results from this replication largely matched the findings from the initial investigation, though the replication of the critical finding itself was mixed. Even with the critical finding, though the single-statistic interaction was not significant, the planned comparisons at each set size did support the initial authors’ claim that the retro-cue benefit exists at all set sizes except for set size 1. In addition to finding support for this principle, we ran the remainder of the same statistical sets as the original authors, and found similar results (see Figure comparing the replication and original). First, there was a main effect of cue type (retro cue > simultaneous cue) across memory set size as a whole [F(1,17) = 66.02, p < 0.0001], and as mentioned above, planned comparisons at each set size showed that this difference existed at all set sizes but set size 1. Moreover, there was an interaction between set size and cue type [F(1,17) = 3.19, p < 0.21], but no such interaction existed once set size 1 was removed from the analysis, providing additional evidence that set size 1 is the outlying set size, which does not exhibit the retro-cue effect [F(4,68) = 1.59, p = 0.21). Further analysis also resulted in full replications when it came to the main effects of stimulus type (accuracy was higher with color than with shape, F(1,17) = 89.92, p < 0.0001) and memory load (accuracy was higher with smaller loads over larger ones, F(5,85) = 180.46, p < 0.0001). Figure: The pattern of results is largely the same for the original and replication studies. In both cases, retro-cue performance is better than simultaneous-cue performance at all set sizes except for set size 1, and the magnitude of this benefit is largely consistent across set size within a stimulus type. Interestingly, whereas in the original study the benefit provided by the retro-cue interacted only marginally with memory load when set size 1 was included, the effect was much more robust here. We suspect this can be accounted for by the larger sample size (18 > 12). It is also important to note that due to simultaneous key strokes, certain trial data was occasionally shifted in the experiment program and manual error correction was necessary. This occurred in a total of 5 trials across all participants. The overall success of replication helps in accumulating further evidence for the retro-cue phenomenon.

decisions.quote: Discussion Summary of Replication Attempt The main aim of this study was to test whether an interaction between PM cue dimension and compatibility would predict the mean proportion of missed PM cues, in a three-way mixed ANOVA including also ongoing task as a between-subjects factor. This result was partially replicated: the interaction between PM cue dimension and compatibility was strongly significant, however it was qualified by a three-way interaction with ongoing task, revealing that the effect was present only for participants in the location task condition but not for participants in the direction task condition. Also several, but not all, secondary results were successfully replicated and in addition some effects that were not present in the original paper resulted significant in this study (this might be partly due to the bigger sample size, and henceforth greater power, of this study, N=95, compared to the original study, N=40). Commentary As summarized above, the key result was partially replicated.

decisions.quote: Discussion Summary of Replication Attempt The analysis confirms the original effects observed by Vul and colleagues (2008), namely that selection is (a) suppressed (efficacy), (b) delayed (latency), and (c) diffused (precision) in time during the attentional blink as demonstrated significant main effects of each of these factors and by a significant three way interaction between SOA, measure (efficacy, latency, precision). The other main finding by Vul et al (2008) was that efficacy, latency and precision can be dissociated by their time course such that each effect returns to baseline at different SOA. These effects were also found as illustrated by comparing the figures from the original study with the replication results in Figures 1 and 2. While there are subtle differences in the specific results for the effects of suppression, delay and diffusion, the overall pattern of results is essentially the same between the original and replicated results. In sum the results from the original study by Vul et al (2008) were successfully replicated.

decisions.quote: Discussion Summary of Replication Attempt Our results provide mixed evidence regarding the role of extremal edges defined by texture alone in depth perception. In our data, EE2 (a region with an extremal edge on the shared contour, and on the opposite contour) was chosen as closer than other textures, paralleling the original study. Likewise, when both regions had only one extremal edge, the one with the extremal edge on the shared contour was more likely to be perceived as closer (EE1>Convex1), though this effect was weaker than in the original study. However, we were unsuccessful in replicating the finding that EE1 regions are perceived as closer then Convex2 surfaces; this test asks whether an extremal edge on the shared contour is the dominant cue to depth in these stimuli, when pitted against the number of extremal edges (i.e. half cylinders are seen as close than quarter cylinders), and so constitutes a stringent test of the prediction. This final test was our a priori selected target of replication.

decisions.quote: Discussion Summary of Replication Attempt The central goal of the current study was to investigate the replicability of the effects reported in Experiment 5 of Demany et al. (2008). We were able to replicate the significant main effect of ISI which showed that performance worsened as the interval between a chord and tone increased. Next, we also replicated the non-significant main effect of N, showing that N did not significantly affect performance. Finally, in contrast with the original study, we found that the effect of ISI on performance did not differ between chords with small or large N. Given that these data follow two of the three trends found by Demany et al. (2008), the current study qualifies as a partial replication. Commentary While this study qualifies only as a partial replication, we believe it is important to point out that the significant ISI x N interaction found in Experiment 5 was not anticipated given the prior trends and conclusions from Experiments 1, 2, and 4. Indeed, it was reported to only have occurred due to "unexpectedly high d' when N was equal to 1 and the ISI was 0 ms". Importantly, the central finding of Experiment 5 was replicated. Therefore, we believe our data to be mostly in line with the effects found by Demany et al. (2008).

decisions.quote: Discussion Summary of Replication Attempt The present replication of Experiment 8 from Murray et al. (2008) replicated some of the components of the original results. Our findings did support the original hypothesis that participants with low self-esteem are significantly less willing to provide actual behavioral support to their partners when they perceived higher criticism from their partners as opposed to when they did not perceive that their partners were critical. decisions.quote: Confirmatory analysis The data from 20 participants were analyzed in order to attempt to replicate the original authors’ primary finding that older children performed at above-chance levels on “where” trials, answering an average of 1.41 out of 2 trials correctly, t(31) = 3.23, prep = .97. In our replication study, a one-sample t-test showed no such trend, M = 0.625, t(7) = -1.426, p = .197. Younger children (M = .833) also did not perform at above-chance levels on “where” trials, t(11) = -.804, p = .438. Similarly, neither the older (M = 1.125) or younger (M = 1.08) group performed at above-chance levels on “there” trials, t(7) = .357, p = .732 and t(11) = .364, p = .723, respectively. At one point during the planning of this replication, independent measures t-tests comparing younger versus older students on the number of correct “where” trial and “there” trial responses had been identified as the key finding. These analyses also showed no differences between younger and older children on “where” trials, t(18) = .627, p = .539, nor on “there” trials, t(18) = -1.04, p = .918. Discussion Summary of Replication Attempt Unlike in Nurmsoo and Bloom (2008), the confirmatory analysis for the current replication attempt did not reveal above-chance performance by older children on “where” trials. Thus, it is clear that we failed to replicate the original study’s finding.

decisions.quote: Replication of “The sunny side of fairness: Preference for fairness activates reward circuitry (and disregarding unfairness activates self-control circuitry)” by G Tabibnia, AB Satpute, MD Lieberman (2008, Psychological Science) Anastasia Rigney Taru Flagan Jennifer Beer beerutexas@gmail.com Introduction In their original paper “The sunny side of fairness: Preference for fairness activates reward circuitry (and disregarding unfairness activates self-control circuitry,” Tabibnia, Satpute, and Lieberman (2008) discuss the difficulties in separating the desire for fairness from the desire for material gain in the context of economic decision making. Accordingly, there had been little research on whether fair proposals produce positive emotional response due to its inherent fairness regardless of material gain. The original authors suggest that ultimatum games that require bilateral bargaining allow these motives to be tested independently. In this replication of Tabibnia et al. (2008), we sought to reproduce the methodology used in the original paper. The present work was conducted as part of the Reproducibility Project: Psychology which asks volunteers to replicate the final study in their chosen paper. Therefore, this is a direct replication of Experiment 2.
